title: Survivors under the snow
teaches: What lived through the 1980 blast at Mount St Helens

blocks.text: At 8:32 on the morning of Sunday 18 May 1980, the north side of Mount St Helens slid away and the volcano exploded sideways. The blast, a cloud of hot rock, ash and gas, flattened about 600 square kilometres of forest in a few minutes. Geology's branch on the Cascades tells how it happened. This lesson is about what came after.

When ecologists first flew over the blast zone, it looked dead. Near the mountain the forest had been stripped away to bare ground. Further out, millions of trees lay flat in rows, all pointing away from the crater, under a grey blanket of ash. Further still, trees stood dead, scorched brown. Many expected that life would have to start again from nothing, arriving from the forests outside, as it had on the bare ground below Glacier Bay's ice in lesson 14.

blocks.caption: Trees in the Smith Creek valley flattened by the 1980 blast, all lying the same way, away from the crater.

blocks.text: Within weeks, they found they were wrong. Charlie Crisafulli, a young field biologist who would spend the next forty years on the mountain, and Virginia Dale, a plant ecologist, were among those who walked the blast zone in 1980 and 1981. Green shoots of fireweed and thimbleberry were pushing up through the ash from roots that had survived underground. Here and there were small fir and hemlock trees, alive and undamaged. Mounds of brown soil from below the old surface lay on top of the grey ash, pushed up by pocket gophers, small burrowing rodents that had spent the blast in their tunnels[^gophers].

The survivors had one thing in common: on the morning of the blast they had been sheltered. Roots, bulbs and burrowing animals were below ground. And much of the high ground, especially slopes facing north, was still under deep spring snow. The snow took the heat of the blast and spent it melting, while the plants underneath stayed at freezing point, and then it melted slowly away from the young trees it had covered. In lakes still covered with ice, fish, frogs and salamanders came through alive.

The blast's date decided much of what lived. In mid-May the snow still lay deep on the higher slopes, many animals were still in their burrows for the end of winter, and the summer's migrant birds had not all arrived. The blast also came early on a Sunday morning, when the loggers who worked in those forests were at home; that saved people rather than plants, but it shows how much hung on the hour and the day.

blocks.caption: The blast zone as a grid, crater at the bottom, with its zones of pumice, trees blown away, trees flattened and trees killed standing. Late snow on high and north-facing ground shelters what is under it. Choose the month of the blast and watch plants spread back from the survivors. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then compare a May blast with one in midsummer

blocks.text: In the model, as on the mountain, survivors scattered through the blast zone speed recovery enormously, because each one is a source of seeds and shoots in the middle of the bare ground, not kilometres away at the edge. Only on the Pumice Plain directly north of the crater, where hot flows of pumice buried everything metres deep, did nothing survive at all. The next lesson goes there.

The forest ecologist Jerry Franklin, who worked at the mountain from the first summer, gave a name to what the survivors showed. Disasters, he argued, rarely wipe the slate clean. They leave **biological legacies**: living plants and animals, seeds and roots in the soil, dead trees standing and lying, and soil itself. What survives decides how fast and in what direction the land recovers. After St Helens, ecologists looked again at fire, windstorms and floods, and found the same[^franklin].

The idea changed forest management. Logging that clears everything leaves few legacies, and in the 1990s foresters in the Pacific Northwest began to leave standing trees, dead snags and logs in cut areas on purpose. Around the mountain the contrast can still be seen. Much of the blast zone became a national volcanic monument in 1982 and was left to recover without planting[^elk], while on the timber company land next to it the fallen logs were salvaged and young trees were planted in rows[^salvage].

blocks.title: Outside
points: At the Johnston Ridge or Windy Ridge viewpoints, look across the blast zone for patches of older trees among the young ones. Many of them are survivors from 1980, which were small and buried in snow on the morning of the blast. Notice which way the slopes they grow on face.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the survivors
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What sheltered many of the plants that survived the blast?
choices: Late spring snow, and being underground
The shade of the standing forest
items.why: Roots and burrowing animals were below ground, and deep snow covered high, north-facing slopes.

items.ask: What did pocket gophers do for the recovering ground?
choices: They pushed buried soil up through the ash
They ate the seeds of weeds
items.why: Their mounds of old soil on top of the ash gave seeds a better place to start.

items.ask: Why would a midsummer blast have left fewer survivors?
choices: The snow that sheltered plants would have melted
More hikers would have trampled them
items.why: In August little snow lies even on high, north-facing slopes.

items.ask: Why do survivors scattered across the blast zone speed recovery?
choices: Each is a source of seeds and shoots in the middle of bare ground
items.why: New plants need not wait for seeds to arrive from the forest at the edge.

choices: What survives a disaster: living things, seeds, dead wood and soil
The first new species to arrive after a disaster
The trees planted to replace a forest after a disaster
items.why: Franklin's term. What a disaster leaves behind decides how the land recovers.

summary: **The 1980 blast flattened about 600 square kilometres of forest.** At first the land looked dead.
**Within weeks, survivors appeared.** Fireweed from roots, buried young firs, gophers' mounds of fresh soil.
**Snow and soil sheltered them.** Late spring snow covered high and north-facing slopes; ice covered the lakes.
**Timing decided much.** A midsummer blast would have found less snow and fewer animals underground.
**Survivors scattered through the zone speed recovery.** Each is a source of seeds in the middle of the bare ground.
**Franklin called them biological legacies.** What survives a disaster decides how the land recovers.

franklin.title: Legacies after fire
franklin.text: After the Yellowstone fires of 1988, ecologists found that even in severely burned areas, pine cones that open in heat, surviving roots and unburned patches seeded most of the recovery. The pattern of burned and unburned ground mattered as much as the total burned.

salvage.title: Two kinds of recovery
salvage.text: The planted company forest grew trees faster, and its young conifers soon closed over. The monument recovered more slowly and more patchily, with more kinds of plants and animals in its open, mixed ground. Each shows something different about how a forest regrows.

gophers.title: The gophers
gophers.text: A pocket gopher spends nearly its whole life underground, eating roots and bulbs. On the ash-covered ground its mounds mixed old soil, with its fungi and seeds, into the new ash, and plants grew best on and near them.

elk.title: The elk came back
elk.text: Elk walked back into the blast zone within a year or two, eating the new growth and carrying seeds in their dung and fur. The herds grew large on the open, grassy ground, which is now some of the best elk range in Washington.
